about.pitch: Meet Felipe, a Senior Software Engineer focused on building tools, pipelines, and systems for VFX, animation, and real-time content. A natural problem solver, he builds technology that removes complexity from creative workflows, giving artists and teams more time to focus on what they do best. With over five years of commercial software engineering experience and an MSc in Computer Animation and Visual Effects, he combines software engineering with hands-on experience in computer graphics, rendering, simulation, and pipeline development.

dccTranslation.title: DCC Translation Pipeline
dccTranslation.description: Maya to Unreal Engine USD translation pipeline.

media.alt: Dcc translation Unreal Engine 5 imported items
Dcc translation Unreal Engine 5 imported scene

blocks.text: A validation-driven Maya to OpenUSD pipeline for standardising scene publishing between Maya and Unreal Engine. Maya scene data is extracted into a lightweight, DCC-independent SceneGraph, validated against configurable rules, converted to USD, and published with structured metadata.
The pipeline separates each stage of the publishing process:

items.title: Scene Extraction
items.text: Maya DAG hierarchy, transforms, geometry and metadata are converted into a SceneGraph.

items.title: Validation
items.text: YAML rule profiles check the scene before publishing.

items.title: USD Export
items.text: The validated SceneGraph is translated into a structured OpenUSD stage.

items.title: Publishing
items.text: Publish metadata is generated and translation activity is recorded.

items.title: Unreal Engine
items.text: The resulting USD stage can be imported while preserving scene hierarchy and per-object separation.

blocks.text: The SceneGraph acts as the intermediate representation between Maya and OpenUSD. It stores the essential structural data required for cross-DCC translation and USD stage construction, keeping the core publishing system independent from Maya.
Scenes are validated using configurable YAML profiles covering:

items.text: Naming and hierarchy
Supported node types
Transforms and geometry
Scene scale

blocks.text: The Maya plugin provides the artist-facing validation and publishing workflow, while a CLI exposes the same functionality for command-line workflows.

Publishing generates structured metadata and records translation activity through interchangeable registry backends. SQLite supports local workflows, while MongoDB provides a database-backed option. The project also includes automated testing with Nox and mayapy and a drag-and-drop Maya installation workflow.
The completed pipeline provides a standardised path from Maya scene data to Unreal Engine through OpenUSD, with validation and publishing handled as separate stages.

items.title: Validated publishing
items.text: Invalid scenes can be identified before USD export.

items.title: DCC-independent translation
items.text: The SceneGraph separates Maya extraction from USD publishing.

items.title: Structured USD output
items.text: Scene hierarchy and per-object separation are preserved for Unreal Engine.

items.title: Tracked publishing
items.text: Publish metadata and translation activity are recorded through SQLite or MongoDB.

items.title: Multiple workflows
items.text: The system is accessible through the Maya plugin and CLI.

wavefront.title: Adaptive Wavefront Path Tracer
wavefront.description: C++17 CPU wavefront path tracer investigating adaptive scheduling for coherent rendering.

media.alt: XYZRGB Dragon Scene USD scene render

blocks.text: A CPU-based wavefront path tracer developed for an MSc research project investigating whether adaptive workload scheduling can improve execution coherence and rendering performance. The renderer uses C++17, OpenUSD and Embree, with a modular scheduling framework that allows different workload ordering strategies to be evaluated within the same rendering pipeline.

The research focuses on the shading stage, where rays can diverge across materials, textures and shader operations. The project investigates whether runtime information can be used to make better scheduling decisions than static material or texture sorting.
The renderer separates path tracing into independent stages connected by work queues:

items.title: Scene Loading
items.text: OpenUSD scenes are loaded into internal geometry, material, texture and camera representations.

items.title: Ray Generation
items.text: Primary camera rays are generated and stored in the RayQueue.

items.title: Traversal
items.text: Embree performs BVH intersection and produces shading records for rays that hit the scene.

items.title: Scheduling
items.text: The ShadingQueue can be reordered using the selected scheduling policy.

items.title: Shading
items.text: BSDF evaluation, direct lighting and secondary ray generation are performed on the reordered workload.

items.title: Iteration
items.text: Secondary rays are returned to the RayQueue and the process continues until paths terminate or reach the maximum depth.

blocks.text: The renderer uses separate RayQueue and ShadingQueue structures implemented using a Structure of Arrays layout. This separates traversal data from shading data and provides explicit points where workloads can be reorganised before execution.

items.title: RayQueue
items.text: Stores ray origins, directions, throughput, pixel coordinates and path depth.

items.title: ShadingQueue
items.text: Stores hit positions, normals, material and texture IDs, and path information required for shading.

items.title: Scheduling
items.text: Policies generate a sorted index order before the queue is materialised for shading.

blocks.text: Keeping scheduling separate from the queue implementation allows different scheduling strategies to be evaluated without changing the rest of the renderer.
The renderer implements a physically based path tracing pipeline with direct and indirect lighting, supporting diffuse, metallic, dielectric and emissive materials.

items.title: Next Event Estimation
items.text: Explicitly samples light sources to estimate direct illumination.

items.title: Multiple Importance Sampling
items.text: Combines light sampling and BSDF sampling using the power heuristic.

items.title: Adaptive Sampling
items.text: Uses Welford's online algorithm to estimate per-pixel convergence and stop sampling pixels once their estimated error falls below the threshold.

items.title: Russian Roulette
items.text: Terminates low-contribution paths while maintaining an unbiased estimator.

blocks.text: Four scheduling policies were implemented to compare static and runtime-aware workload organisation:

items.title: None
items.text: Preserves the original traversal order and provides the baseline.

items.title: Material
items.text: Groups shading records by material to improve shader and material-data locality.

items.title: Texture
items.text: Groups records according to texture access to target texture cache locality.

items.title: Cost-Benefit
items.text: Combines material grouping, spatial ordering and runtime shading-cost estimates to prioritise work according to expected contribution relative to execution cost.

blocks.text: The Cost-Benefit scheduler is the main research contribution. Runtime measurements are collected while rendering and used to estimate the cost of shading different materials and textures.

A per-material cost estimate is updated using an exponential moving average. The scheduler combines these estimates with accumulated ray throughput to calculate the expected contribution of shading work relative to its execution cost.

items.title: Runtime cost tracking
items.text: Measures shading cost during rendering and updates the estimates for subsequent scheduling passes.

items.title: Work prioritisation
items.text: Higher contribution relative to estimated cost receives higher scheduling priority.

items.title: Spatial ordering
items.text: Morton ordering is used within material groups to retain spatial locality.

items.title: Cost-aware termination
items.text: Russian Roulette incorporates estimated material cost into path termination decisions.

blocks.text: The scheduling policies were evaluated using two procedural OpenUSD benchmark scenes under identical rendering configurations. The Mixed Scene combines different geometry, materials and textures, while the Dragon Scene uses a higher triangle count with a more consistent distribution of geometry and materials.

items.title: Sample counts
items.text: 256, 1024, 2048 and 4096 samples per pixel.

items.title: Scheduling policies
items.text: None, Material, Texture and Cost-Benefit.

items.title: Measurements
items.text: Shading time, pipeline time, scheduling overhead, execution coherence, cache-line homogeneity and image difference.

items.title: Repetitions
items.text: Three independent runs were performed for each configuration.

blocks.text: Cost-Benefit produced the lowest shading time across both benchmark scenes and consistently improved on the unscheduled baseline. The improvement increased with rendering workload, reaching its largest reduction at the highest sample count.

items.title: 8–10% lower shading time at 4096 samples
items.text: At 4096 samples and 1080×1080 resolution, Cost-Benefit reduced shading time by 7.7% in the Mixed Scene and 9.6% in the Dragon Scene compared with the unscheduled baseline.

items.title: Improved execution coherence
items.text: At 4096 samples, Cost-Benefit produced average material run lengths of 1474.5 records in the Mixed Scene and 1560.7 in the Dragon Scene, compared with 2.9 and 2.8 for the baseline.

items.title: 98.9% material cache-line homogeneity
items.text: Cost-Benefit achieved material cache-line homogeneity of 98.9% in the Mixed Scene and 98.8% in the Dragon Scene, compared with 21.9% and 19.0% for the baseline.

items.title: Lowest total pipeline time
items.text: Cost-Benefit achieved the lowest total pipeline time across the evaluated experiments. The largest reduction occurred in shading, while smaller improvements were also observed in traversal. Scheduling introduced additional cost for runtime analysis, but this remained small relative to the time saved.

items.title: Minimal image differences
items.text: Comparison with the baseline produced mean luminance differences of 0.0088 in the Mixed Scene and 0.0100 in the Dragon Scene. Most differences were concentrated around the ceiling light and did not change the final rendered result.

blocks.text: The results show that execution coherence alone was not sufficient to obtain the best rendering performance. Material scheduling achieved similarly high coherence, but Cost-Benefit performed better by incorporating runtime execution cost into the scheduling decision.

This project was completed as my MSc research project in Computer Animation and Visual Effects at Bournemouth University, achieving a Distinction with a final grade of 87. The result reflects the substantial research, engineering and evaluation required to take the project from an initial research question through to a complete working renderer.

mocap.title: Motion Capture Retargeting & Cleanup
mocap.description: Unreal Engine 5 motion capture retargeting and cleanup pipeline using IK Rigs, IK Retargeter, Control Rig, and Houdini.

blocks.text: A motion capture retargeting and cleanup pipeline developed for the group project Eternally Dancing. The workflow uses Unreal Engine 5 to retarget AI-generated motion capture onto production characters, clean the animation using Control Rig, and refine the resulting motion in Houdini.

My contribution focused on investigating the motion capture workflow, defining the UE5 and Houdini pipeline, building the retargeting setup, and cleaning the resulting animations for use in the final project.

The project initially investigated several approaches for generating motion capture data. After testing multiple AI-based solutions against sample dance sequences, QuickMagic was selected for its ability to generate motion from recorded footage and refine tracking points before export.

items.title: Capture
items.text: Recorded dance footage following the requirements for the selected motion capture workflow.

items.title: AI Tracking
items.text: Generated animation from the recorded footage using QuickMagic.

items.title: 2D Refinement
items.text: Corrected tracking points before exporting the resulting animation.

blocks.text: The motion capture output was imported into Unreal Engine 5 and transferred onto the project's characters using the IK Rig and IK Retargeter systems. This allowed the captured performance to be adapted to different character skeletons while preserving the original movement.

items.title: IK Rig
items.text: Configured the source and target character skeletons with IK systems for pose adjustment and retargeting.

items.title: IK Retargeter
items.text: Mapped the captured animation onto the project's characters while maintaining the original performance.

items.title: Control Rig
items.text: Used Control Rig inside Unreal Engine Sequencer to manually refine poses and correct sections of the animation.

blocks.text: The retargeted animation was cleaned directly in Unreal Engine using Control Rig and Sequencer. Keyframes were added where required to correct the motion and refine larger body movements.

items.title: Ballet Animation
items.text: Refined the retargeted dance performance using Control Rig and Sequencer.

items.title: Stretch Animation
items.text: Applied the same cleanup workflow to a second animation used for the character transition.

items.title: Reference-driven Cleanup
items.text: Used the original performance as a reference when correcting poses and movement.

blocks.text: After the initial UE5 cleanup, the animations were transferred to Houdini for further procedural refinement. Houdini provided additional tools for inspecting and modifying the complete animation sequence.

items.title: MotionClip
items.text: Used MotionClip to inspect the complete animation sequence and edit motion procedurally.

items.title: Motion Processing
items.text: Used nodes such as Stabilize Joint and Smooth to refine the resulting animation.

items.title: Validation
items.text: Applied the cleaned animation to the project's 3D characters to verify the final result.

blocks.text: The final workflow separated the motion capture process into dedicated stages, using each application for the tasks it was best suited to handle.

items.title: Motion Capture
items.text: Recorded performance footage and generated the initial animation.

items.title: QuickMagic
items.text: Generated and refined the AI motion capture data.

items.title: Unreal Engine 5
items.text: Retargeted the animation using IK Rig and IK Retargeter, then performed manual cleanup with Control Rig.

items.title: Houdini
items.text: Performed additional procedural refinement and validation using animation processing nodes.

blocks.text: The project also involved supporting the wider production with procedural tools and technical fixes in Houdini.

items.title: VEX
items.text: Implemented VEX logic to dynamically control elements of the butterfly effects used around the character.

items.title: Butterfly Movement
items.text: Adjusted movement and normal orientation to prevent butterflies from behaving erratically around the dancer.

items.title: Transition Effects
items.text: Added controls to keep butterflies facing forward and maintain spacing during the transition spiral.

snowglobe.title: Real-Time Snow Globe Simulation
snowglobe.description: Real-time particle-based snow globe simulation using Position Based Dynamics, WebGL, and Three.js.

blocks.text: A real-time snow globe simulation developed to investigate particle-based techniques and Position Based Dynamics in a browser-based environment. The system combines Verlet integration, iterative constraints, spatial hashing, collision handling, and GPU instanced rendering to simulate thousands of particles interactively.

The simulation supports two particle behaviours: a marble mode designed around rigid particle collisions and a snow mode that produces more clustered and cohesive movement while maintaining stable real-time performance.
The simulation is structured as a sequence of particle update, neighbour search, constraint solving, collision handling, and rendering stages.

items.title: Integration
items.text: Verlet integration updates particle positions using current and previous positions.

items.title: Spatial Hashing
items.text: Particles are assigned to grid cells so neighbour searches only evaluate nearby particles.

items.title: Constraint Solver
items.text: Position Based Dynamics iteratively resolves particle overlaps and maintains minimum separation distances.

items.title: Collision Handling
items.text: Particles are constrained against the snow globe and simplified scene collision geometry.

items.title: Rendering
items.text: Three.js and WebGL render the particle system using GPU instancing.

blocks.text: The simulation uses Position Based Dynamics to maintain stable particle interactions by directly correcting particle positions rather than relying on traditional force-based integration. Multiple solver iterations are performed each frame to reduce overlap and improve collision stability.

items.title: Verlet Integration
items.text: Calculates particle movement from the difference between the current and previous positions.

items.title: Iterative Constraints
items.text: Repeatedly corrects particle positions to maintain separation and stable interactions.

items.title: Damping
items.text: Reduces excessive bouncing and helps particles settle after collisions.

blocks.text: Neighbour searches are accelerated using a spatial hashing grid. Instead of checking every particle against every other particle, each particle searches its current cell and the surrounding 26 cells.
This reduces the number of collision checks required as particle counts increase and was an important part of maintaining interactive performance with thousands of particles.
Two particle behaviours were implemented to explore different material responses within the same simulation framework.

items.title: Marble
items.text: Uses more rigid particle interactions, producing faster movement and more visible bouncing during collisions.

items.title: Snow
items.text: Reduces relative particle movement and encourages particles to settle together, producing a denser snow-like appearance.

blocks.text: The simulation runs entirely in the browser using TypeScript, WebGL, Three.js, and React Three Fiber. GPU instanced rendering allows thousands of particles to be drawn using a shared mesh and material, reducing the rendering overhead associated with individual particle draw calls.

items.title: GPU Instancing
items.text: Renders the particle system using instanced geometry to reduce draw calls.

items.title: Interactive Gravity
items.text: Rotating the snow globe changes the direction of gravity inside the simulation.

items.title: PBR Rendering
items.text: Uses physically based materials and HDR lighting for the final snow globe scenes.

blocks.text: Performance was evaluated by increasing the number of simulated particles and measuring the resulting average frame rate. The tests show how simulation and neighbour-search costs increase as particle density grows.

The simulation maintained interactive performance across the tested range, although performance decreased as particle counts increased. At higher densities, neighbour searches and collision solving became more expensive, making spatial hashing and GPU instanced rendering important for maintaining real-time interaction.
